utterances.text: All right. It's not three questions. You have reduced this to three hypotheses. Have we clarified that matter now?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were three hypotheses. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that on the 24th of March, 1999, a war started, waged by NATO against Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you assume that a war is a very complex situation and from many points of view it is also chaotic, and it is therefore difficult to simplify matters and to reduce everything to three hypotheses only, the way you had done it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We look at the data with the idea that there may be some broad patterns in the data on refugee flow and killing, and those patterns may be quite clear. The clarity of the patterns may be surprising in light of what seems to be chaos. I think that this is one of the points of science, is to find patterns and clarity in the midst of chaos. When we look at these patterns, they are in fact much less chaotic than would be implied by the question. These are the bases for our conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you assume that such a complex and chaotic situation, as war is, cannot be reduced and simplified to three hypotheses only. Can you assume that people were fleeing from the war, the war, the war that included all sufferings, all fears, not only one of the three fractions that you turned into hypotheses and that you wish to single out? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Rephrase the question. May there be other reasons than the hypotheses which you used for people to have fled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there may. These seemed to us the most obvious hypotheses since these were the three parties with significant arms involved at this time. However, this method does not exclude the possibility that there may be other causes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that the subject of your statistical survey was actually to establish the common cause of exodus, the common cause, the reason. That is the wording you used, I believe.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used the word "common cause." We did not use the phrase "establish." What we are looking for in the analysis of common cause is we are looking for patterns which move together over time and space. Such coherence, the connection of patterns over time and space, correlations, in the statistician's language, strongly suggest the existence of a common cause. They do not establish it, nor do we make the claim that that is established. We conclude, based on such a strong suggestion, that such a cause existed. But again, the scientific language is quite formal here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. This is not even contested that there was a common cause, but did it occur to you that the common cause of the exodus was war? You said there was a cause and then this cause was stopped. There was a war going on from the 24th of March onwards and then that war stopped. While the war was on, the exodus was going on as well. When the war stopped, the exodus stopped. Did it occur to you that this common cause was the war, not this - how shall I put it? - this quest and elimination between and among only three hypotheses that you have put forth by simplifying an extremely complex phenomenon as war is?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is the question that when the war stopped, the refugee flow and killing stopped? Is that the question? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking you, did it occur to you that this common cause was the war? Because everything happened from the 24th of March when the war started. And then when the war ended at the beginning of June, when this common cause ceased to exist, all of this stopped. The war stopped; all of this stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, it did occur to me. Excuse me. So we tested it. We tested the idea given the data we had. In particular, we were interested in what happened during the ceasefire period, the ceasefire declared unilaterally by the Yugoslav government - excuse me - on -- again, as I said, on the evening of the 6th of June, the early morning of the 7th. So I looked at the four-day period from the 7th to the 10th, and again as we've discussed, there was relatively little -- there were relatively few killings or - and little refugee flow. The graphs are clear about that. What's fascinating to me is that the number of -- the number of KLA activities recorded and the number of NATO airstrikes documented again by the Yugoslav government and press sources, both of those patterns increase dramatically, doubling and tripling relative to their numbers in the earlier period. So it in fact was a unilateral ceasefire during this period since these other two parties dramatically increased their activity at the time when refugee flow and killing declined to tiny fractions of their earlier levels. So while war, in a very broad and, in my opinion, vague sense may be a cause, what is clear is that the statistical relationships are not equal here. One party declared a ceasefire, the refugee flow and killing declined drastically, but at the same time, KLA and NATO activity increased drastically. There is no corresponding increase in the patterns of killing and refugee flow. This helped us to be increasingly confident in our rejection of the hypotheses that I earlier stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have been talking about simplification in terms of three hypotheses of this common cause that is called "war." It lasted, it produced these consequences, it stopped, and then the consequences stopped. Are you aware of the fact that in this war, it was not Yugoslavia that attacked itself?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a conflict that -- between NATO and Yugoslavia, and there was clearly an insurgency by the KLA. What language in formal legal terms you use, Mr. Milosevic, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. It seems to me that what is suggested by the question is that the people might have fled because of war and not a single factor of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How could you simplify those complex factors into three simplified hypotheses? That seems to be the question. Could you answer it? Could you help us in that sense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do so by means of a theory, which is that if -- if -- in the presence of war, there would be -- certain things would occur, and those things should leave us some way to count them. Some of them would be countable. We look for things, in fact, that are countable as indicators of our -- of our theory about what's going on. The indicators we found were battles between the KLA and Serb forces. This seemed to be a reasonable indicator of the local presence of this broader idea called "war." Similarly, casualties inflicted on Serb forces by the KLA would be an indicator of the presence of this broader thing called "war." I don't claim that these indicators, the things we can count and measure - deaths, battles - I don't claim that these indicators encompass the complexity of this enormous idea, but they should be present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. You may go on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So then these first two hypotheses, that is to say NATO and the KLA, is it clear to you that, in this war, NATO and the KLA were acting with the same objective in mind? Did you give any thought to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you assist or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not give any thought to that idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now, now can you look at this idea, this concept that NATO and the KLA worked with the same objective in mind, that is, a single hypothesis, the concerted activity of NATO and the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He did not consider that. Therefore, he cannot give evidence about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Even if we are not bringing together many things but, rather, separating them, we are looking at a complex issue such as war. Even if we were not to link them together at all, do you think that this question boils down to combat action only of the Yugoslav army and police, of the KLA, and of the NATO bombers respectively? Or this complex phenomenon called war, does it contain many other phenomena that also affect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have made this point. He has answered the question. Now, kindly move on to another topic or we'll bring this to an end.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the core of the matter, because the witness himself has said that it is certain that there are many other elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am going to mention some elements now, and you're going to tell me whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said there may have been other elements. These were the three that he concentrated on. Now, if you want to put some other elements, you can, but the witness may not be able to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I want to put a question to the witness. So other phenomena that affect people are, in my opinion, political means, propaganda, threats of the KLA, orders of the KLA, the media war that waged, et cetera, and the leaflets, the black and red ones that were thrown, in the colour of the Albanian flag through which the citizens were ordered to leave the territory of Kosovo. War is not only a bullet and a bomb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Ask a question. I told you before, it's not a time for making speeches. Now, the question appears to be this: Were there, in your view, other matters or did you consider other possible causes for, it seems to be, the refugee flight, namely, propaganda and threats of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was an occasional topic of discussion among my co-authors and myself. We did not consider the effect. What we did, however, is observe that propaganda is unlikely to cause killing in the same way, and thus when we found the close correlation, the correspondence between the patterns of killing and the patterns of migration, we felt that that -- that the propaganda explanation was unlikely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why are you simplifying matters? Why are you reducing it to propaganda only? I'm also talking about threats that were not empty threats only, because the KLA killed many Albanians as well in order to discipline them. I'm talking about orders issued to the population to leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with it one by one. The next question is threats. Did you consider threats made by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We considered it unlikely on the same basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this has no effect, propaganda, calls, threats, orders issued by the KLA to the population to leave the territory. Is that the way it is in your opinion? Or the media war either that was part of this war as well?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said and I think as is clear from the report, we did not consider these hypothesised causes presented by the question in a direct way. However, given what we have considered, it seems to me that they are unlikely causes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But let's think logically about this. You have linked all reactions to combat action only, to fire, as if we were talking about a herd that reacted to shooting only while the shooting was going on, as if it weren't people who were at stake, who think about all these things, who have reason, who are susceptible to pressure, to instructions, to media manipulation. Homo sapiens think and bear in mind all these elements, not only the momentary situation when somebody is shooting and somebody is killing. Do you bear in mind this complexity of the situation that you have simplified, reducing it to these three hypotheses only?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly we considered the effect of something that has happened in the recent past in addition to the events that are occurring at the immediate time. We had an extended discussion of this yesterday around the statistical term of a "lag." Again, that means that we considered the effect of KLA activity and NATO airstrikes in the previous four days, the current period, two-day period, and the previous two-day period. It is in this way that we have considered time. I did additional analyses that go under the statistical language of - pardon the jargon - autocorrelation, which looks at patterns over time, looks for those sorts of relationships. The one that I found that was meaningful in this analysis was the immediately-prior period. It only appeared to be meaningful in the variables we discussed yesterday about the KLA having -- relating to migration in certain regions at certain times, but that's where it appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For example, are you aware of the columns of Albanian refugees who were returning to their villages after the bombing, and they were bombed along the way by NATO as they were returning? Do you think these were messages as well, that orders had to be carried out, that Kosovo had to be left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so. I think the question is am I aware that NATO bombed Albanian refugees on the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That seems to be the first part, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some incidents of that kind reported in the Yugoslav government and press sources. We counted them in our data.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you about the effect of such a message, when a column of peasants who are going back to their village are bombed and at the same time there are orders and requests put through the media that Albanians should leave Kosovo. Did you take that into account as an effect of this message or did you only add up the persons killed by NATO in these columns?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not take that into effect. And to clarify, the analysis of the NATO airstrikes is not number of people killed; it's number of airstrikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The number of airstrikes is something that we will look at later, but by enumerating all of these individual elements of war - far be it that I have managed to mention all of them - the question is: Is it clear enough that looking at all the phenomena related to war in their cumulative effect, can be defined as a common cause and that this cannot boil down to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have been making this point over and over again. The witness has dealt with it. Now, in light of your application for more time, we're prepared to give it to you until the adjournment. There will be no more time after that. It will give you nearly three hours to cross-examine this witness, which is more than adequate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have two or three minutes of personal privilege if we're going to continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn for five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. --- Break taken at 12.29 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we are discussing the inviability of these simplified premises in statistical analysis, even if the data were accurate, and they simply cannot be, in view of their source. Do you suppose that all these complexities of phenomena encompassed by the war, as a fact, as a phenomenon, should be explored for a scientist to arrive at valid conclusions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This study sets out very specific hypotheses and it makes conclusions based on the best data available to us. I am not competent to enter into a larger methodological or epistemological debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If we are talking about statistical data, does the fact that this report is based on records made by immigration officers on the Morina border crossing and research made in refugee camps in Macedonia and Albania, and even Bosnia and Herzegovina is mentioned, does this put a question mark over the validity of your report and its conclusions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And does the question arise in your mind, as the person who researched this: Who are these administrative officers on the border crossing of Morina who were able to engage so quickly after the aggression in drafting these records? And you said the largest report came in the first stage, in your own words.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the regular border guards who worked that post. They may have been supplemented with guards brought from other posts, given Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that this post was experiencing such heavy flow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At this first stage, do you think that the issue of this readiness and alertness of border guards or clerks was important, the fact that they were ready to deal with this very large inflow and quickly make records?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if they were ready in some sense. They were able to do a good job within the limitations of their personnel and capabilities. I discussed in some detail yesterday how I evaluated their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did it cross your mind that it can only be explained by the fact that the appearance of refugee columns were preplanned and organised in advance in order to create an impression around the world that they were a product of an ethnic cleansing campaign, and other things that you are claiming, rather than the war in all its complexity, as is obvious?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several questions there, some of which I think I answered earlier, about the war's complexity. But on your new question, did it occur to me that this was preplanned, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me: Who could have expected these records to be accurate and truthful, knowing the objectives of the Albanian secessionist movement and the attitude of Albania towards Serbia and Yugoslavia and the so-called Kosovo problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely what I asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who could possibly expect these records to be truthful, knowing the objectives of the Albanian secessionist movement and the attitude of Albania towards Serbia and the so-called Kosovo problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's dealt with these questions. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have said that the research which has allegedly been conducted in refugee camps were based mainly on interviews. Who conducted these interviews?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We reviewed the sources of the information in these reports several times. But to review again, in answer to this question: The surveys conducted to supplement the migration analysis were conducted both - excuse me - first, by teams that I organised myself; second, by interviews conducted on a random sample population basis by Physicians for Human Rights; and third, interviews of refugees conducted by Human Rights Watch. In the second phase of the study, the analysis of killing patterns, there are three interview-based sources in addition to the exhumation records. The first were the interviews conducted by the American Bar Association, Central East European Law Initiative and their partners; second, interviews conducted by Human Rights Watch; third, interviews conducted by the OSCE. These are the interviews conducted in order to support this -- in order to do this. They were conducted by very different organisations, at different times and places, and yet they tell a remarkably similar story.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We are talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, just a minute. Who were the people interviewed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kosovar Albanian people who were either in refugee camps or back in Kosovo, depending on which phase of which survey we're discussing. They were Kosovar Albanian civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if this is what Mr. Milosevic was inquiring about, but I would be interested, in any event, to know whether your analysis took account of the -- what would be a natural prejudice on the part of the interviewees.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not take account of it in a direct sense; however, statistically what I think is interesting is that our method for the killing analysis depends on finding the same people reported by the same or different witnesses to different projects. We found a relatively high rate of those overlaps among different reporting processes. That is to say, the same victims appeared in Human Rights Watch interviews, OSCE interviews, ABA/CEELI interviews; and in exhumation records, not always in all of them, but you see a very high rate of overlap among two systems or among three systems. If people were making this data up, they would have had to coordinate a fabrication among more than 15.000 interviews conducted over an almost two-year period and given to four different -- or three different organisations, as well as fabricating exhumation records. The level of fabrication required is, in my opinion, deeply implausible. It is in that way that, at a statistical level, we are confident of the robustness, that is to say, the resistance of our findings to fabrication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think precisely the opposite. I think they were coached, because the statements, depending on their education attainment level, were identical. But let us make one thing clear. We are talking about an interview as a methodological procedure, requiring a very qualified and unbiased approach. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the purposes to which we put these interviews, all that I required was that people write the story down. We're looking here just for a list of people described as dead, and the time and place of the witness's best recollection of where and when that person was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know very well, being a sociologist, that the interview, as a methodological procedure, cannot be conducted with one single question: Please describe what happened.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interviews were done in different ways. As you'll find in Appendix 1, there's some discussion of the interview process. The Human Rights Watch interviews were conducted by a qualitative method, which proceeds along the lines of the interviewee's story. The ABA/CEELI and OSCE interviews were conducted using a -- to use a tiny bit of jargon here, a semi-structured interview process, which asked open-ended questions, for example: Why did you leave your home? The witness would report, in some phrases, his or her reply. Those would be recorded. The interview - or excuse me - the questionnaire process for the OSCE and the ABA/CEELI teams was quite similar. Physicians for Human Rights used a much more tightly structured interview process. Again, the only use we put those interviews to in this work was to calculate from the story the time it took from someone's departure from their home to crossing the border. That's the only use we put those interviews to in this study. Although the interviews that I designed and that we did in the refugee camps in Albania and other refugee-gathering locations in Albania, although that was a much more elaborate interview, the only use we put it to in here was to calculate the transit time, as I just described - the time it takes people to get out from their home, to get to the border - as well as to provide a check on the distribution of people's origin locations over time, as reported in the border data. These methods are described in "Policy or Panic?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely what you have just mentioned, that you used their statements to establish the time of departure and the time of border crossing. You said yesterday you had established that the overwhelming majority crossed the border the day following the date of departure. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry. What we established is that the overwhelming majority of people had crossed the border on the same day -- not the overwhelming majority. More than half the people crossing the border on any given day left their homes that same day. That was our -- what we discovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is even less likely than what I mentioned in my question, because that Morina crossing, and even the Vrbnica crossing, make it implausible for anyone to cross the border on the same day as leaving their homes, if we bear in mind the enormous mass of people. Do you know anything about the distance, the difficulties of the journey? Do you understand that it's very unlikely that such a great number of people at that first stage crossed the border on the same day they left their homes?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two independent counts of the number of people crossing the border at that point. The numbers largely agree. And when they disagree, the numbers reported by the UNHCR and OSCE observers is always higher, always greater than what was registered by the border guards. So I can't address the plausibility of whether it happened except to say that I think that all available evidence says that it did happen. So plausibility is no longer an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that plausibility is not your area of expertise, but it's -- when I'm saying that it's unlikely for them to have made a move on the same day as crossing the border, then it puts a question mark over their other statements if something that is physically impossible is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ask a question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can we consider, in view of the fact that we agreed that the interview as a methodological procedure has to be conducted neutrally and by experts, by qualified people, can we consider as neutral the way that interviews were conducted by the party which perpetrated the aggression?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's not a proper question. THE ACCUSED [Interpretation] The question is very clear. I don't know if it was put correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can change the suggestion that it was conducted by the party which perpetrated the aggression. That is not a proper question. What you can deal with, Dr. Ball, is this: Do you consider as neutral the way in which the interviews were conducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the purposes of obtaining the data required for this analysis, the interviews were neutral.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in which way -- except for the statements of refugees, what else is there to support the claim that only a few number -- that only a small number of Kosovar Albanians fled Kosovo because of NATO bombing and that it followed certain constant patterns so it had to be coordinated? What is there to support this claim?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe that is a conclusion from my first report. However, I would point to the current report that we're looking at as evidence here and say that we have now given the analysis of refugee flow a thorough statistical test by two different measures and found conclusively and consistently that NATO airstrike patterns do not explain the patterns seen in refugee flow. Furthermore, the close correlation of refugee flow with killing patterns over both time and space suggests more strongly than in the first report that there is some sort of coherent or common cause of the two phenomena.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but NATO's airstrikes were also coordinated with the activities of the KLA on the ground, and they constituted one comprehensive form of attack on Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That is a speech. Now, have you got any more questions? Because the time is practically finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The main conclusion that Yugoslav authorities planned and carried out a campaign which was centrally organised in order to ethnically cleanse from Albanians at least certain areas of Kosovo, as claimed, is not proven in any way except by hypothesis. So I'm asking you: If the Yugoslav authorities planned and carried out a centrally organised campaign, where is that plan? What is it called and who made it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My conclusion here and the conclusion of myself and my co-authors is that the evidence is consistent with the hypothesis that Yugoslav forces conducted a systematic campaign of killings and expulsions. Again, we have found the evidence to be consistent with the hypothesis, and I've described in some detail why and how we reached that conclusion. That is the extent of my expertise, is to speak to the statistical evidence related to the hypotheses which we proposed. Beyond that, I'm unable to comment further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you are aware of the statement of one of NATO Defence Ministers, the German Minister, Rudolf Scharping, who said that there was a plan, the Horseshoe Operation, and this claim was later refuted even by his own associates as a lie. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I read about it in the press, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can't deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. If there is no such plan, and there is none, how can this campaign be conducted in a planned and organised manner?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's here to give statistical evidence, which he's given. He cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you explain that if everything you are presenting in statistical terms -- if I may ask you to agree with certain things, if we added up, in terms of maps 1, 2, 3, and 4, it turns out that 471.000 people crossed over into Albania. So where is the difference, the difference of 850.000 people mentioned in the indictment? It is unimaginable that all of them crossed over to Macedonia or Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number to which you refer includes border crossings other than the one that I studied. The number of total refugees, 850.000, does not come from my most recent work. I can't comment on it. However, it's important to remember that refugees went places other than just Macedonia. They went to Montenegro. Some went to Bosnia-Herzegovina. So should you seek a larger number, it seems appropriate to look at all the destination countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So it's not within the area of your interest. But dealing with what you have, how do you explain the large difference in the number of refugees, according to your maps 1, 2, 3, and 4, 471.000, and the diagram which indicates 248.000 people? How do you explain that difference?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where does 248 come from?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I mean the chart that you show for the first, second, and third stages.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you give me a --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have the right -- I don't see how you marked the chart, but this is a rectangular chart. 25th March, 12th April, 24th May. That is the chart which shows in the first stage, second stage, third stage, and when you add all the numbers up, you get 248.000.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me which report it's in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you assist with this at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what he's referring to. I would look at it, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the witness can't assist with this matter. Now, you've got one more question to ask him and then we must adjourn.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have more than one question, Judge May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have given you a time limit and it's now come, so you've got one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, this is very important. One of your claims is that NATO bombing did not produce waves of refugees, while your own data go against it, because the percentages of NATO airstrikes coincide with the numbers of refugees by stages. I will read to you the data. You said the number of targets -- you mentioned 942, with the proviso that at the first stage the number of targets was 541, and that is from the 24th March to the 6th of April. Out of the total number of targets, that is 58.55 per cent. And in that first stage, from the 24th of March to the 6th of April, you quote in your text that 236.000 people fled, which means at the first stage, according to your own text, amounts to 61.14 per cent, which is an extremely large degree of coincidence. 58.8 -- 55 per cent of targets --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... just break this up so the witness can follow it. Now, what is being said? Just break it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you can refer me to what you're looking at; which report, what page number, what table?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I made for myself, because I have no resource to any assistance here, I made copies of your report, but you know that what you wrote in your text that in the first stage, from the 24th of March to the 6th of April, 236.000 got out. In the second stage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just pause -- pause there. Do you agree with that figure? Just a moment. Just a moment. Let him deal with it. Do you agree with that figure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is approximately correct. We'd need to refer -- I don't want to be held to that number without checking it here, but I think that's approximately correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You can check it on the tape. I'm reading your data. I'm not reading my own. So in your text, you're talking about 236.000 in total out of which in the first stage 236.000, in the second stage 83.000, and in the third stage 67.000, and the total is 386.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Two hundred and thirty-six thousand in the second stage. Does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. 83.000 in the second stage. Does that sound about right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the first stage, 236.000. Is that correct? The second, 83.000; and in the third, 67.000. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just let the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those are approximately correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, look at the number of targets, bomb targets, NATO airstrikes. 924, as you put it, in the first stage, 541 in the second stage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Let's break it down. It's suggested there were 924 in the first stage. Does that sound about right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Where are you getting that data, please, so we can refer to it here? I don't remember that. I don't think -- the bombing numbers that I know of are much smaller than that. Remember, we're counting airstrikes, not people killed or something else. If you could give me a direct reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You wrote in your text a total of 924 as the number of targets in Kosovo. 924. In the first stage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where will we find this in the text?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In his own text, Mr. May. I can't leaf through it now. You can check this data. It can be found in the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He doesn't agree with you. But will you come to the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what is the essence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take the time to hear me out. And if you don't believe this data is in his own text, you can check it later. In fact, he himself can do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We have verified -- deal with the number of refugees. Now we are dealing with the number of targets, 924 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes. What is the point that you're making to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have been saying this: Out of the refugees number, in the first stage -- 61.14 per cent crossed over in the first stage, because 236.000 out of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That sounds right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the same time, the number of targets in the first stage is 58.55 per cent. 58.55 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means that the percentage of refugee outflow in the first stage almost completely coincides with the number of targets in the first stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We have the point. What is your comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know where his number of targets comes from. That --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about the percentage? Almost 58 per cent was bombed during the first phase? That seems to be the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 58 per cent of what? Are we talking that 58 per cent of the airstrikes occurred in the first stage? That is certainly Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. false. If we mean that 58 per cent of the municipalities in Kosovo were bombed during the first phase -- is that what the question is? That's possible. We'd have to look at that municipality by municipality. The question, though, it seems to me, for a causal argument, has to do not with whether it occurs in a long period but whether there is a sufficiently close correlation in time and place of bombing intensity and refugee outflow to hypothesise or to sustain the hypothesis that the bombing pattern has caused it, and we have conducted that analysis and rejected that hypothesis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you take it any further than that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn now. After the adjournment, we will hear the amicus.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You won't let me put any more questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's right, we won't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn until twenty to three. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.12 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was my understanding that you would not let me continue my cross-examination. I just want to give some explanations that the witness requested, and I did not have these things at hand. 924 bombings. That particular figure comes from maps under B, from the first report. 924 bombings: In the first stage, 541; in the second one, 241; and in the third one, 142. And the percentages calculated showed that the percentages of refugee flows and the percentages of the targets engaged totally coincide. They correspond to each other, actually. Secondly, the chart that the witness asked me about is the chart that is Chart 1, also from Annex 1 of the first report, and the total is 248.000: In one -- in first stage, 164; and in the third stage, 49 [as interpreted]. And Maps 2.1, 2.3, and 2.4, the total is 471.000. The second stage is 331 and the last one is 67 [as interpreted]. So according to the maps, it is one figure, and according to the charts, it is another figure. In addition to that, the witness said that he did not operate with the figure of 850.000 refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've had your chance to explain the matter, and that's sufficient. We're going to hear -- no, no. We're going to hear now some cross-examination from the amicus. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Dr. Ball, have you ever appeared as an expert witness in court before?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The data that you used for the compilation of your report and research, is that available for an independent inspection?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The data for the migration study were placed on the Internet -- were placed on the Internet over a year ago. The data on killing were disclosed to the Defence along with the report. The information on KLA activity and NATO activity were derived, as I described, primarily from open sources, which we detailed. And so we believe that the data are available to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is there any aspect of the data that is not available? Is there any aspect of your research that is unable to be disclosed or is unavailable?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 45 per cent of the sources used to analyse the KLA data are the -- are in the domain of the Office of the Prosecutor, and I would direct the inquiry to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I just help with that, because I was going to deal with it in any event. That material, subject to any redactions for proper reasons that might be approved by the Chamber, will be available to any expert who wants to have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to your research and study, what would be the leading international journal in which a study such as this would be published for reading and inspection by other members of your profession?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably demography, the journal of -- one of the journals of the Population Association of America.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Has your report been sent to that publication for publishing?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not right now, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you intend to do that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some portions of the -- I'm sorry, there's a ringing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. There's a technical hitch, obviously, going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It can't be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Apparently the technician is on his way. Yes. It seems to be -- try it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't think that was me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Dr. Ball, just to repeat my last question ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'll try again, shall I, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Dr. Ball, just repeat my last -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have something coming into the courtroom, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Dr. Ball, I'll just repeat my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to have to adjourn. Ten minutes. --- Break taken at 2.52 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, it's apparently been fixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It sounds all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will move on to another subject as I know time is of the essence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I should say that we will in fact sit until 5.00 because we've had these breaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want to deal with general matters concerning data, Dr. Ball. Data you have used depends upon the accuracy of the account or record given; that is right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the data depends -- every piece of data has some precision associated with it, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the record made of data has to be accurate as well?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The record made of data. I'm not sure what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's just take a simple example in this case of the border guards in Morina. The account given to them must be accurate.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what people say to the border guards when they say, "This is my address," yes, that must be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. The date they left the country, that must be accurate?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be accurate when it's written down by the border guards on the form, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And for any study such as yours, you are only able to act upon the records what you're given?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not quite right, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this concern that you're raising is the point of a kind of study called sensitivity analysis. And we have done substantial sensitivity analyses in both the migration study as well in the present study, looking for, quite literally, the sensitivity of our findings to imprecision in the data.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The record made by the person writing a document upon which your data is based must also be accurate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it mustn't. Well, that's not quite right, actually. I'm sorry, I will have to refer to my previous answer. We -- it is certain that some data are in error. The question is then: Does that error impact our conclusions? That is the point of doing a sensitivity analysis. If the findings are not subject to change, the conclusions are not subject to change as a result of making very, very different kinds of assumptions about the precision of the reporting, then we say the conclusions are robust to imprecision in the data. So it -- I think it's your term "must" that I'm objecting to. That's not quite correct, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to the raw data, the forms completed by the Albanian border guards, are they available for inspection?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not currently available for inspection. I could -- I had, at the time that I obtained the records, a brief note of agreement with the Albanian government that I would maintain those records in confidence. I could inquire of the Albanian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. You've heard the allegation in this case that these could be fabricated.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard that allegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And a part of that allegation, if it's to be carried forward, would require examination of the documents that you yourself have relied upon.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be one way to test the allegation. However, I would refer you to Appendix A in the "Policy or Panic?" study where we tested the patterns in the border records against the surveys and found them to tell substantially the same story. We have several different surveys. We looked at some of the most important patterns we found in the border data and we found the same patterns. So I think that for statistical purposes we have already investigated the possibility that there might be some problem, of whatever kind, with the border data, and we have rejected that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Moving on now to an aspect of your analysis, which was the dates of the migrations. As I understand it, the data that you have worked upon has been compiled by an assumption of the period of time taken for each of those individuals to migrate from their village through to the border crossing of Morina.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As I take it, you have made an assumption.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't make an assumption. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me clarify that. We looked at the survey records that I've described in the past and we determined from the survey records how long each of the respondents in the surveys had been in transit from his or her home village to the border point. So we then have a set of transit times that correspond to a particular -- leaving a particular village at a particular time. Understand so far? I'll explain how this applies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I just clarify one matter: Is it an estimate, then, of the time of each individual, when they would have left the village to have got to the border crossing?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's closer, yes, yes. We estimate, actually, for each person crossing the border, how long ago they left their homes, and we make that estimate based on the survey information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it's that migration which -- or time of migration that really underpins your research, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, originally I thought it would, which is why I did a sensitivity analysis precisely on the question you're asking, and we simulated very, very different kinds of migration or transit time structure from people's departure to the point of getting to the border. That distribution, the amount of time it takes the people who cross the border on a given day - How long ago did they leave? Some people left today, some people left yesterday, some people left the day before - that, to a statistician, has a certain shape. I simulated -- and in the report here that's been on the Internet for a year and a half or a bit more, I simulated very, very different distributions. I said: Well, what would happen if the transit time process was completely different? And I did that in six different ways. All of those results were nearly indistinguishable from the original. It turns out that the transit time process makes very little difference to the conclusions which have been presented in this report and subsequently in the report which my co-authors and I have presented to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One other aspect of data as well that I'd like to deal with here is the dates of killings and identities of who has been killed, because, would you agree, this seems quite an important part of your research?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dates of killings are quite important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The names are important, but I think less so for technical reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall we just start with date of killing.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As I understand it, there are instances that you have relied upon when people have given a date, and that's been a date with a named person that you've been able to positively identify.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There have been other occasions when accounts have been given of a body being referred to by the side of the road or in a house, which is a death that has formed part of your statistical material.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's clarify that a bit. The people who were identified without name we referred to as the anonymous victims. The anonymous victims played a role in this analysis only for one purpose. It's important to be clear. For this purpose only did we use the anonymous victims, and that was to establish that removing all the anonymous victims who could possibly have been accounted for by name as a named victim, there nonetheless remain quite a few; at minimum 2.000-some anonymous victims. The only use we put this information to is to say there have to be more. There have to be more than the named victims. We do not believe that the anonymous victims provide an adequate basis for a statistical estimate. They do not provide sufficient information for us to do analysis. So we used only the named victims. But we observe that net of the named victims, nonetheless, many thousands of anonymous victims remain who had names. These people had names, they are just not documented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to deaths as well, was it possible to distinguish in your research as to which of the victims were Serbs, which were Kosovo Albanians, whatever ethnic group they may be? Was there any distinction you are able to draw within the figures that you have given?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could you explain further.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We attempted to identify names that appeared to be ethnically Serb names. Because this was a study -- this is a study of ethnic Albanians, it was important to exclude the Serb victims from the calculations. They would get their own calculations in a different study, I presume. But for this study, we wanted to exclude them from the lists. We sought lists of surnames, and when we -- surnames of Albanian and Serb surnames, and when we found names, we checked each of the names on our lists against the Serb -- the list of Serb surnames, and when we identified them, we removed them from the list and did not use them in the calculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the identification process that you underwent had to be accurate to get the right people for your statistical study.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The identification of the ethnicity of their name?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The people who identified them had to be right about the person they had identified.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And any problems associated with the identification process might cause your attribution of those particular deaths to be flawed.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, "might" encompasses, to a statistician, a wide range of probably. I think it's possible that misidentification could increase the error range, the margin of errors that we have reported. However, I doubt it, because in order for the misattribution to affect these results beyond the error that we have already calculated, those misattributions would have to be not only very large in number but they would have to be very systematically distributed through these four independent projects. The combination of those two assumptions seems to me very unlikely. So I do not consider it probable. It is possible, perhaps remotely possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've heard about carbonised bodies, bodies that are unrecognisable. How were they dealt with in your study?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if they were unrecognisable, then -- and they were identified, for example, by an exhumation, then they would be part of the deaths -- the bodies exhumed there were not identified. In reference -- in Appendix 1, you will find that we excluded approximately half of the exhumation records because they did not have names. So a carbonised body that was never identified would be in that category. On the other hand, if the person had been seen to have been killed by someone else, if there was a witness to the death and if that witness subsequently reported that death to one of -- either the OSCE or Human Rights Watch or ABA/CEELI or its partners, that death would appear in the lists. If we can take a second on this observation, it's actually quite insightful, because this is precisely what a statistician is looking for by the combination of data with different kinds of data that are going to be excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: So if, for example, a death occurs and there are no witnesses to that death except the perpetrators, that person may nonetheless appear in an exhumation, but of course, he or she would not appear on a list created by witnesses because no one would have witnessed it. The example that has been posed by the question is the opposite problem; a death which cannot be identified in exhumation but might well have been identified by witnesses. To a statistician, these are biases or exclusions or data that can't get into a list which complement each other when you combine the lists. This is exactly the thing which this method, the multiple systems estimation, is strongest at, is identifying those sorts of conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Moving on to another subject, I'd like us to turn to page 11 of your final report, and Figure 8, which is the table headed "Timing of KLA attacks with killings and refugee flow." Have you got that before you, Dr. Ball?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Looking at this table here in relation to your particular study, killings preceded or coincided with peak in relation to the KLA, from your study, am I right in thinking matched 38 per cent of your material?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite. It matched 38 per cent of the -- in 38 per cent of the municipalities, of the 29 municipalities, the -- there is one or more KLA attack or interaction with Serb forces in the four days preceding the peak of refugee flow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So that appears --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, killings. Ten for refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was dealing with killings.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That appears to be more than a third of the instances; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a third of the municipalities, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And in relation to the refugee flow, that again is slightly more than a third.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: A third of the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Turning to page 12, Figure 9, the timing of NATO airstrikes with killings preceding or coinciding with the peak; 10 per cent.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of municipalities, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Refugee flow, again with municipalities, in relation to NATO airstrikes preceding or coinciding with the peak; 31 per cent.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You make the distinction with municipalities. Why do you make that distinction?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Why do I make -- why do we use municipalities as the unit of analysis?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because here we were seeking a method to present this kind of -- present an analysis of these statistical relationships in really quite straightforward terms without using more complex statistical techniques. In this way, we were really also looking for something that would be comparable to the municipality level analysis done in the "Policy or Panic?" study, the earlier study. This seemed one way to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You've chosen to represent your material by the use of a graph. If we look at page 9 and other pages within your report, you use the graph system for the presentation of your material.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The graph system?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We use graphs, yes. That's a standard statistical technique.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. There are other standard statistical techniques. One can Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. use a column diagram of blocks. You can use a pie chart.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can. However, in standard statistical practice, representing something over time is done with a line where time is on the horizontal axis. Other representational schemes are possible for other kinds of data but would be inappropriate for these data.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we are dealing with amounts or quantity so that we could look at this material, we could use a block system, column graph.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: For quantity, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where the -- that would be most appropriate where the distinctions were by category, but that's refinement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we were to look at this material in that form, we would see in certain municipalities that the KLA killings were the more dominant cause for the refugee flow.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the interpretation would never be about the cause. The interpretation would always be that there seemed to be a higher level of KLA killing in some areas, or KLA interactions, battles, or casualties inflicted on Serb forces. Those would be higher in some municipalities and lower in others, and in some municipalities that would coincide with higher levels of other phenomena.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just taking your material, and in relation to it, I'm not saying whether it's good or bad, but in relation to your material, there have been killings caused by KLA activity that caused refugee flow?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we have a confusion about what the header "Killings" means here in this table. Are you referring to Table 9?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. The "Killings" column does not refer to KLA killings; it refers to the killings we have estimated -- or actually just counted in this case. These are not estimates, as we discussed in my direct exam. These killings are only those which we counted in our 4.400. So that's distinct from the KLA killing measure which we have discussed in the context of the tests, for example, in Figure 8, or also in Figures 10 and 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in relation to your conclusion, you have written that you believe the activity of the Serb forces was the primary cause. If you want the reference ... I've had to shorten my questioning, so I can't put my finger on it, but --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I can help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our conclusion is that the evidence is consistent with the hypothesis that Yugoslav activity was the cause of these -- of the killings and refugee flow of Albanian -- of Kosovar Albanians. We do not refer to that being the proof nor do we say that it establishes that; rather, we find them to be consistent with the hypothesis. These statistical methods do not prove things, although they can assist us in rejecting claims. So I think it's useful to be as formal as possible in the scientific language here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just one other matter I want to deal with, which is the border crossing of Morina, wherever that might be. The issue doesn't change. You have taken the documents from one place. We know from the evidence there are six or seven other border crossings that might be used by refugees. Why do you say that just taking the one place is able to provide a statistical analysis for the whole region?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I covered this in my direct testimony, but to repeat that, there were two reasons. First, by my estimate presented in the first report, "Policy or Panic?" I believe that somewhat more than half of all Kosovar Albanians who left Kosovo did so through this point. Thus, this is clearly more important than all the other exit points combined. Second, I examined survey information from other places and considered what the likely pattern from those places would be. The likely pattern discovered that -- that I found in the survey data suggests that patterns of refugees entering the other countries would be similar to the pattern I found in -- on the refugees that crossed through the data I did examine directly. So both because I have more than half the data, and second, because what other information available suggests that other places are similar or the same, leads me to conclude that this analysis, using this data, does represent the most likely patterns of refugee movement. That was where we had to leave it in the first study. Subsequently, of course, as I've been discussing for the last two days, the information on killing patterns again correlates quite closely to the original migration patterns. This provides us with an external, completely separate statistical validation of the original findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But it does depend upon an assumption that, first of all, the border crossing that you have chosen -- and there may be a dispute about the place and whether it's the right place - I don't know - but it depends upon the assumption that you do have up to half the total figure of people migrating through that particular channel; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not exactly an assumption; it's more like an estimate, because we do know something about the numbers of people who crossed through other points. We are not -- we do know something. We know something from the counts kept by the Albanian border guards at the two other primary crossing points; we know something, although, in my opinion, with quite a bit of error, we know something about refugees who crossed into Macedonia; and we do know something about refugees who crossed into Bosnia; and we know a little bit, with less certainty, about those who crossed into Montenegro. So knowing those other things, I think we can narrow the claim I've made from an assumption to, I think, a reasonable estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, just let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- ask the witness a particular question, since it's before me here. One of the reasons that you advance as to why you used Morina is you say the other information that you have in relation to other crossings is more or less the same, or is the same. I mean, have you exhibited that in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's statistically similar, I think is what I would say; not the same but, rather, that it would not, if we added it, change the findings. I have not exhibited it in the current report, because I did not anticipate this would be of so much question. It is, however, documented in my earlier report, in the "Policy or Panic?" report, which we looked at this morning. It is discussed in some detail there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. I would have thought that that was a matter of some importance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If it is an issue that's investigated, is the data able to be scrutinised upon which you have said you have based your estimate?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said in the answer to the first data inquiry, the data from the migration report have been available on the Internet for over a year. So the data analysed in this report and in the report I've presented here, these have been available for some time. The other sources that I used - not the surveys, but the other overall counts - are available -- they're cited in the OSCE report and are available from the UNHCR. UNHCR made many of those estimates. The survey data are not all mine to disclose. That which is mine, I could make available. I have not yet, simply because there hasn't been time. It's complicated to make sure that the confidentiality concerns are all addressed. But the other data that I used for this process from Physicians for Human Rights and Human Rights Watch, again, I have under confidentiality agreements, so I would have to inquire of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice. Fairly briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I have a number of matters, and I think they are important, and I must seek to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dr. Ball, much of this can be dealt with by yes or no answers, and if you would be so good, I'd ask you to provide those answers whenever possible. Just dealing with the questions of the amici, first of all, the report to the Court, has it until now been kept confidential because it's appropriate to go to the Court first?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has been -- it has not been disclosed publicly. I have shared it with the reviewers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is now available publicly?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it on a stack in the lobby. Many of them are being taken away. It is quite publicly available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just yes or no. The Albanian records, in respect of which there's an agreement, are you physically in possession of a disk or whatever that has photocopies of those records so, subject to the agreement, you can provide them?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I have scanned images. I will have to look.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may "Policy or Panic?" now be produced as an exhibit and given an exhibit number? It's been extensively referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 69.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dealing with the particular question you were asked by Mr. Kay about the dates upon which people left and the accuracy of that, apart from estimating the time that might have been taken from one village to reach a border, did any of the questionnaires actually contain the question: "When did you leave?"

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so you were acting on the basis of that information as well?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the basis for the estimate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Has any reason been advanced to you as to why people should give -- they might give inaccurate, but why they should give intentionally dishonest reasons about the date they left their premises?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look -- and this is the last question from the amici and then I'll come back to the accused's questions.
