Can we look at Table 8, which, to remind the Chamber, is the table built on the raw data -- not the raw data, but the elementary data rather than the enlarged figures. Table 8, or Figure 8, on page 11. Thirty-eight per cent, thirty-four per cent, and slightly different figures for deaths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you put that on the ELMO, Figure 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can page 11 go on the ELMO first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Ball has it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we could have the ELMO up, from the booth, please. If the booth could operate the ELMO, the overhead projector. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Looking at this, the figures of 38 per cent, 34 per cent, you said just over a third, is it appropriate at this table to look at figures in that very elementary way, as percentages, when one's looking at the sort of issues you're looking it, or is there another argument, another approach that one should take?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Percentages seem fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The majority in the left-hand column but one, 63 per cent, do not precede or coincide with; in the right-hand case, 66 per cent - the total of 38 and 28 - do not precede or coincide with. The significance of that, and the argument to be derived from it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said in direct, that tends to reject the hypothesis that KLA attacks are responsible for killings or refugee flow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's now go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, excuse me. Before we move on, could you put Figure 9 on page 12 on the ELMO, because we are dealing with the problem. And our learned friend dealt with it briefly, but my question yesterday wasn't yet answered, so I'd like to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. That was my error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No problem. Do you see the Figure 9? So am I right in understanding that your conclusion is that given the fact that NATO bombing preceded the refugee flow only in nine municipalities out of 29, then NATO bombing could not be a plausible cause for the refugee flow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This table begins my conclusion in that direction, Your Honour. It combines with later analyses to bring us to the final conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. So the question yesterday was that -- yes. Let me put it this way: It seems that the analysis may not take into account the effect that an attack in one municipality have on one another. Hypothetically, a situation could have arisen in Kosovo whereby a KLA attack or NATO bombing strike took place on a particular day in one municipality and that, as a result of that, the people, Kosovo Albanians in the neighbouring municipality, fled their homes. Has such a possibility been taken into account?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not do a neighbour-by-neighbour comparison, as your question suggests. Instead, in the following analysis, the analysis of the residual patterns, Figures 10 and 11, we treated Kosovo by regions much larger than single municipalities, and I thought by -- what a statistician would often do with a question such as the one you have posed is to look at a bigger area, to expand the boundaries outward, thereby reducing the number of little boundary-crossing incidents that would perhaps muddy the analysis as you have suggested. So by expanding the areas in the analysis of residual patterns, I believe I would have captured the subtle differences across regional -- excuse me, across municipal boundaries that I think you're investigating, you're thinking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. My next question is: I wonder if you can name those municipalities by the name, by their names. In, for example, Figure 9, there are nine municipalities in which the NATO bombing preceded the refugee flow. Could you tell the names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not from memory, sir, Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you have the data.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, you are dealing with 29 municipalities in your research, but the indictment against this accused relates to the incidents which took place only in 13 municipalities among them. So if the nine -- or the municipalities here are all included in the 13 municipalities which is dealt by this indictment, can we say then that, in those municipalities, the NATO bombing was the primary cause for the refugee flow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would answer no, and my logic there would be expressed in the addendum that the -- that the Office of the Prosecutor requested from me and that we looked at briefly at the end of my direct exam yesterday. In that, I argued, and the Defence brought it up on cross at some length, that finding the presence of a particular phenomenon, in this case, say, KLA attack or bombing, finding the presence before the peak of the resulting phenomena, the hypothesised cause, would not necessarily imply in a positive sense cause. Okay? The absence of the presence of the cause does lead us to reject it as a cause. However, let us imagine that we measure the rising sun every day. The sun comes up every day in every municipality in Kosovo. So if we check for the presence of the sun rising before the peak of refugee flow, we'll find it. The sun will have risen on the day that has the peak refugee flow. However, that tells us nothing about whether the sun caused refugee flow. If the sun had failed to rise for four days before the refugee flow, we could reject the hypothesis that the sun had caused it. However, finding the sun does not lead us to suggest that it was a cause. If that's -- I hope my logic is clear there. But this method is adequate only for rejecting this hypothesis, which I believe it has helped us to do. In order to suggest that there is a closer correlation which might imply cause, we need a subtler, a subtler tool which we attempt to provide in the analysis of residuals in Figures 10 and 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just one other question about method and reports and one thing and another. If the accused or if the amici choose to instruct an expert, not only will you do everything you can to provide materials, but if the expert would prefer to enter into a dialogue with you before coming to court, would you be prepared to cooperate?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under instruction from the Court on how we should control that dialogue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move on to Morina just to make sure we've got this clear. The Morina statistics were what you used for refugee flow. Killing statistics came from much wider sources; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And are not in any way geographically local?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And yet from both the Morina refugee flow figures and from the Kosovo-wide killing figures, you happen to derive very similarly shaped graphs.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Morina itself, did you approach it from Albania or from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two more maps. I'm neutral as to whether they go in as separate exhibits or the original. And I can deal with them very briefly, but I'm sure the Court wants to see them. The first map -- and in each case they are essentially Yugoslav maps. That's right. This one. Original for the overhead projector, for distribution to the Court, and one for me, I think. I'll just keep one. They are originally Yugoslav maps. One at a time. Just put that on the overhead projector. We can deal with it quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They're opened at the right place. They show the road from Prizren down to the west or --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was opened at the right place, usher. Thank you. They're all folded so as to help.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This isn't quite there. May I adjust it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, do.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's to show this piece down here, okay? Yes, that's it. That's it. You may wish to put the point on --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My video channel isn't working. I don't know if anybody else's is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's not waste time. The ELMO should be working, but it doesn't seem to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Morina can be found on this map - thank you very much - immediately to the west of the border between Albania and Kosovo, coming up in the direction that the witness came from from Albania. And the next map which abuts this one and covers Djakovica, with which the Chamber is familiar. They're all opened at the right place for displaying immediately on the ELMO or distribution. Thank you very much. I'll keep one for myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Pausing there. Vrbnica is the other side of the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And Zur, which we've been hearing about, is further along the road towards Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, indeed it is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 71.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Turning to the next map, opened at the right place. West of Djakovica, following the black -- the strong black line that I think is probably a power line but it doesn't matter what it is, towards the -- I'll hold up where it is. There. Just above the strong black line where my thumb is. And in this case, Morina is on the Kosovo side of the relevant boundary, as we can see. All right. That's all for that, but more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the explanation for that? What's the explanation? You've got Morina on the first map, which is Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The witness -- beg your pardon. The accused has been asking about Morina, and I thought it helpful for you to know exactly where it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is another Morina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is the other Morina that the accused is saying is the subject of the corrupted documents. That's his case. I want to deal with that. The exhibits can go off the overhead projector. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who's idea was it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, no. Just -- no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who's idea was it to collect the records, Dr. Ball?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Originally, it was my collaborator Fritz Scheuren and then it was mine, but we were together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. At the time you collected the documents, was there any risk associated with the collection?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were a bit worried, yes. There had been shooting at the border a few days earlier, and the border guards themselves were very reluctant to go to the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the border was indeed unmanned?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was any -- you see, the suggestion is that you were in some way set up. When you went to the border, did you go with guards yourself?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Originally they didn't want to go, but after I just set off Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. walking down the road, they -- one of them kind of trotted after me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there any way you indicated in advance that you were going to take the risk and go into territory where people were shooting to get documents --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- that could be planted there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to the guards, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Other questions about -- other questions about materials. Your Honour will recall that the substantial quantity of material about the KLA that's been referred to, thousands of pages, has only been provided to us and to everybody else very recently and was obviously not available for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The suggestion is that in some way the statistics have been produced to match -- or not the statistics, the data has been produced to match the findings that you ultimately made. So a couple things arise from that. The maps that -- not the maps. The graphs that you've produced, as we have seen, have characteristic and recurring shapes, and what's being suggested is that data has been provided falsely at the border by other people of the Kosovo Albanian persuasion in some way just to create these particular shapes. Is that even possible?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in the most remote sort of science fiction sense is it possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If somebody had a desire that a statistician should produce graphs of this particular form and shape for any particular reason, he or she would then have to generate a whole quantity of false material that would give rise to these statistics; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: A vast quantity of false material, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Distributed according to particular dates and locations and so on?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see anything in the material at all to suggest that such a thing had happened?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And of course, that material, subject to your own confidentiality concerns, is going to be available. You told us that the Physicians for Human Rights data was not used for killings. Why?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they documented only a very small number of killings. That is a limitation of their method.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The accused challenged you with making a selection of what you use insofar as you excluded some and admitted others. On what basis did you make the selection of data that you did use?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the four sources that we used, we chose the biggest ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any reason for selecting against any of the others on grounds of unreliability or method or anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been challenged with the suggestion that this is an innovative method and, therefore, not reliable. As to the component parts of what you have done, do you accept that they're innovative or not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think they're -- each of the pieces are part of the standard tool kit of a competent demographer/statistician.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as to each part of the process, have your calculations been guided by error calculations and by conservatism or not? Just tell us in general.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To what degree have you been cautious and conservative?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Greatly. To what degree implies that I can quantify it. We have made every effort at each decision point to be conservative, and I've described those, I believe, in a question to the Bench -- from the Bench yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused asked you about statistics prepared for Serb casualties, and you spoke of a Serb statistician. Where did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him at a conference of the International Association for Official Statistics in Montreux, Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His name?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slavko Kapron [phoen]. I'm sorry for the pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this a person to whom you provided anything?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave him a copy of the "Policy or Panic?" report, and I told him the data would be on the Internet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you heard any criticism from him of the work that you've done?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear back from him, no. We exchanged business cards, but I did not hear back from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked a couple of questions about the combination of NATO and the KLA as causative of what you discovered. In fact, did your first residual exercise and the two figures to which that gave rise reflect those factors in combination?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it was then subsequently that you broke down the analysis to each factor individually?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To add a technical note, "in combination" to a statistician implies something called an interaction analysis. I didn't do that. The reason is that, in order to do that, you must first have found a significant effect in the individual components, which we did not find. So I did not go the next step.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And of course, there was also a breakdown by regions, as we know.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been asked several questions about the multiple systems estimation. I want you, if you have a plain piece of paper and a pencil, to assist those who are not statisticians in a concept -- I said we might come to this but just help us if you will. If one will forget that it was four topics -- four sources here, assume three, can you, via Venn diagram, for those who are familiar with Venn diagrams, simply display and explain very shortly, as it were, the concept. Not the technique, the concept.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Put it on the ELMO and I'll draw it there. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just, very quickly, if you can draw three interlocking circles, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The idea is the following, that -- let us imagine two studies have been conducted. There are several possibilities about how those two studies might encounter each other in the world. Okay. By "encounter," here I mean document the same deaths. They might interlock or overlap in some small quantity or, hypothetically, they might not encounter each other at all, the two small circles, or one would subsume the other, the concentric circles. Our idea is to look for the entire universe, which here we've labelled "N." I want to know how big all -- how many killings there are in total, but I have two studies, and I use their rate of overlap to estimate the total. The insight we use is that if we saw that the two systems did not overlap at all, the universe would be vast. The two systems would have gone into the field and never encountered each other. If, on the other hand, the two systems went into the field and documented essentially the same lists, we would assume that the universe is only a bit larger than the two projects. By measuring how much the projects have in common, we can use some mathematical insight, some mathematical formalisation of the insight that I've suggested to make an inference, an estimate about the entire universe, which I've labelled here as "N."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And of course, in this case we had four interlocking circles with the complexity that that brings, and the workings of the system is set out in the appendix; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My last few questions, then, are these: The accused has asked you several questions about hypotheses, but correct me if I'm wrong about this. Does the shape of the graphs that the statistics produce lead to the inference that there is either one or more than one cause?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shape of the first graph we looked at suggests that there is one or more causes. As we elaborated and looked at additional graphs, it seemed increasingly likely that there was one common cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's only when you've reached that position, as opposed to an entirely random distribution or a flat-line distribution, it's only when you've reached that conclusion that you seek, for discussion purposes, hypotheses?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as you explained at the beginning of this re-examination, your method restricts itself to excluding, rather than confirming, hypotheses?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Save to the limited extent that you felt able to offer a comment about the Orthodox Easter?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, because of the coincidence there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, the accused, in the last stages of his questioning, asked you questions with a great number of references we weren't able to track. Were you able to track them?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In his last comments, I finally have tracked them down, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you -- and I may be wrong, but it may be that he was trying to suggest that in some way the proportion of deaths matches the proportion of NATO bombs. But insofar as we have his observations - and I can just pull them out in the transcript, I think - he was referring, as we'll remember, to 248.000, 164, Maps 2.3, 2.1, 2.4, and a figure of 471. Can you just deal with those statistics, insofar as you can now recall them, and give your comment on what he appeared to be proposing.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We reviewed, with the Bench assisting, we reviewed the numbers that he proposed, and he was suggesting certain numbers of refugees who had crossed the border during each of the three phases. In that, the numbers that he suggested were roughly correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to any conclusion that he was driving at about the coincidence of NATO and refugee movement or killings or anything of that sort, what do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what we got to after the break was the Defence suggested where he had derived the numbers of bombings. He said it came from Appendix B in the "Policy or Panic?" study. Appendix B begins on page 70. However, he interpreted the little red dots on these maps, which look like this, as bombings. If you refer to the legend, however, to this map, the red dots are not bombings at all. The red dots, in fact, indicate the density of refugee flow. So he counted up the dots that indicate how much refugee flow there had been over time and he discovered that the number of dots correlates with the graph earlier in the book. I had never thought to do this, but it is an interesting check on my work, confirming that these maps do, in fact, represent the graphs earlier, since these graphs and the maps here in Appendix B represent refugee flow, not bombing. In fact, bombing is nowhere on the maps in Appendix B.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And indeed, since it's now an exhibit, since the point has been made, I think that these maps are particularly helpful in relation to the regional variations, aren't they, over time?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was looking at these maps that I just sort of understood this pattern of geographic variance that is now the subject of the later report as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to put one example on the ELMO to explain to the Chamber why you happened to observe, although it wasn't an original intention, you happened to observe this coincidence. Which one? What page?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 72.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Just explain which one.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can look at any of them, but 28 March is a day of particularly high flow. The size of the dots represents the quantity of flow from that point that was reported to the border guards. Again, as we've discussed earlier, these are the dates that we estimate people to have left home. So in this period, most of the people leaving home are leaving in this area in the south and west, relatively fewer in the north and east. Later in the period -- excuse me. In a later period, if I flip forward to, for example, the period in April, we see that the flow is concentrated in the north and east, and there's relatively much less activity in the south and west. I spent several days looking at these maps, and when that occurred to me, when this observation occurred to me, I was able to develop more precise kinds of statistical tests to look for this geographic and time pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's all I ask, although I'll ask Dr. Ball to produce an answer in the form of the most original documentation he has, in copy form, to deal with His Honour Judge Kwon's question. We'll make that available, and he will remain available to assist if other experts are instructed in the way that we've already identified. I observe that there were some questions asked yesterday by His Honour Judge Robinson about potential utility or value of the report, which lay outside the ability of the witness to answer and were probably more questions for counsel. I can deal with them, of course, now, or right at the end of the case, when it's a matter of submissions, as the Chamber prefers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This isn't the time for comment. Dr. Ball, thank you for coming. That concludes your evidence. You're free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May that become an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Next exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 72.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for five minutes before the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: --- Break taken at 4.06 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. What is the point?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a while ago I heard from you that you had extended our working hours today until 5.00. We have already discussed this once. That means that yet again you've decided not to let me get this one-third of fresh air that I have been entitled to, and I consider this to be simple mistreatment of the accused. I'm not asking you for any correction in this regard. But by the way, since last night - actually, all the way until I left the prison - the air conditioning or the air circulation apparatus had broken down. So try to make up your mind and see what kinds of mistreatment you're going to resort to next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm told your time will be extended. There's no difficulty about it. Now, we need to get on with this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you give us your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: My name is Jeremy John Durham Ashdown. I'm more normally known as Paddy Ashdown.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your history is as a soldier, diplomat, Member of Parliament, leader of the Liberal Democrats of Great Britain, member of the House of Lords, and currently High Representative Designate for Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I think I flagged up a couple of weeks ago, or a week ago, I'm going to ask this witness, unless there's any objection, to deal with a single topic in paragraph 3. It may be all we'll ever ask for him to give. In respect of earlier matters, it's indicated that he might be able -- would be willing and might be able to come to give evidence at later stages of this trial, but of course it's inconvenient for any witness to come twice and it might be particularly difficult for him. So I'd ask that this evidence, which doesn't relate particularly to Kosovo - it doesn't relate to Kosovo at all - this rather well-known passage of evidence, and to give it briefly now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Lord Ashdown, in the course of last decade or so, have you taken an interest in the affairs of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I have. I first visited Sarajevo, I think, in July 1992 and subsequently a parlay in August of that year, and since then have visited the region usually, I think, almost without exception, twice every year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With that interest already established, did you find yourself, on the 6th of May of 1995, at a dinner at the Guildhall in London, where you were seated next to the late President Tudjman of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have a conversation with him about the future of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I did. It was an extended conversation. We, I think, if I recall, chatted together, to the exclusion, probably, of our fellow dinner guests, for most of the evening. I think at some stage in it, I asked him to draw on the menu. It was the Guildhall dinner celebrating the 50th anniversary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And can we have a look at a copy of the drawing? Your Honour, the original is held by Registry, in respect of another case. Efforts are already at hand to secure it, but it can't be available now until tomorrow. We'll lay this on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor Exhibit 73.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first page shows the menu, or whatever it may be, for the banquet, and just interpret for us, if you can, the first little markings we see on the left.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's fairly self-explanatory. On the right is the printed menu and on the left is the logo of the event. And then down below -- I don't know whether this shows up, but here are some lines. I had asked President Tudjman if he would draw out for me what he believed to be the future shape of this area of ex-Yugoslavia. He drew the Croatian coast here. This line here represented Bosnia-Herzegovina. This line here represented his idea of the current front line. And he drew an S here, which is what he believed the ultimate position would be. All to the left was Greater Croatia; all to the right, Greater Serbia. All the lines there on the map are those of President Tudjman. The crosses are ones that I had put in, this cross indicating Sarajevo, this cross indicating Banja Luka, this cross indicating Zagreb. And I said to him: "Is that the right positions, as far as you're concerned, in respect of these lines?"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then if we look at the other part of the photocopy of the exhibit, can you interpret this for us, please, and explain who drew what.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I drew -- these are my annotations on the lines drawn by President Tudjman, made immediately after the dinner, so that the English, obviously, sentences here refer to the various lines, this thickened line being the final line of division as he saw it; the towns of Sarajevo, the Krajina, Zagreb, also marked. This line which I put crosses on represents the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I have marked up the Dalmatian Coast and the present front lines. So all the annotations, that is, all the differences between this map and the previous ones are my annotations. As it says on the top here - I don't know if this is yet visible - lines drawn by FT, Franjo Tudjman; annotations by PA, myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Lord Ashdown, you'll see I wait until another language comes to the conclusion so that we don't overstrain the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I'll make sure I do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of this conversation, what, if anything, was said, and on the map, what, if anything, was allowed for Muslim interests and areas?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: President Tudjman said that the Muslims had been incorporated into the territories of Greater Croatia and Greater Serbia, that Bosnia no longer existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there to be any area for the Muslims alone that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now move on to matters in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps the exhibit can be removed from the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of one of your visits between the 20th and 25th of June of 1998, did you meet the Macedonian Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I did. I paid a visit to the Balkans. Wishing to see all sides of the matter, I planned the visit should include Macedonia and Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move on to the detail of this and subsequent meetings, when you went, did you -- in what capacity did you go and how, if properly described, were you to be described?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Well, I went as a -- I suppose you would say a private citizen. I was the leader of a political party. I wished to inform myself of the situation from all sides. I did not go as -- I was not asked to go by the British government, did not go as their envoy. But on this visit, as on previous ones, I felt it right and proper that I should do a report to the then-Prime Minister about the conditions that I discovered and any recommendations that I should have. So the direct answer to your question: As a private citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember -- sorry. You, I think, have kept a diary for many years?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I have, since I first became leader of my party in 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The way in which you keep your diary, is that regular or irregular?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I try to do it every night. I can't say that I'm successful in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that discipline on every night, but I do it pretty well every night. And if there have been major meetings, meetings with the Prime Minister or meetings with other significant figures, I try to make notes immediately on leaving that meeting and then construct my diary from that as soon after that meeting as possible. It may not be that I wait until the evening to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Has part of your extensive diary, subject, of course, to appropriate editorial amendments and corrections and so on, been published?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Indeed, they have, yes. They were published -- first of all it was published in September 2000, and the second volume published in September of last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But material to this hearing, when looking back on a particular visit or a particular meeting, have you had a diary entry that you can refer to to refresh your memory when necessary?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I have had exactly that. In fact, on most occasions when I've been seeking, for instance, to construct the conversation you've just been talking about in relation to Mr. Tudjman, but it applies to all the evidence in relation to the events we are about to discuss, those were recorded either that evening or straight after key meetings, in my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the Macedonian visit in June, can you remember the date upon which - it may not matter particularly - can you remember the date upon which you met the Macedonian Prime Minister --

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I fear I cannot, but it's in my diary. I can certainly recover that, if wished.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With them, the Prime Minister and the foreign minister, what did you discuss?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Well, I think we discussed primarily their concerns. I mean, I had gone there in order to make an assessment of what was, to me, a very dangerous international situation developing because of what was happening in Kosovo, and I wanted to discuss their fears and any recommendations they might have for resolving it. Their fears were that the instability at that stage in Kosovo could, if handled wrongly, lead to a further flood of Kosovar refugees into Macedonia, a country which is already fairly delicately balanced in terms of its ethnic balance as between the Macedonian Slavs and Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you, in the same visit, travel to northern Albania?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I did, indeed, straight after leaving the Prime Minister's office. I drove south to Tirana. On the way, it became evident to me as I thought about the situation that one of the destabilising factors in Kosovo was the activities of the KLA, and that if we were to seek to assist in the stabilisation of an inherently very dangerous situation, we ought to be considering what means we could apply to limit the activities of the KLA and preferably to stop their armed activities. And it was clear to me also that the arms to the KLA were passing through northern Albania, through a widely regarded as very lawless area, in the region known as Bajram Curiju and Trepoje, and I felt that if I was to make propositions about the resolution of this impending crisis, I ought to go and look at this myself, and I arranged to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In northern Albania, in that general area, did you have an opportunity to speak to any refugees?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I did. I spoke to, I suppose, altogether some 40 or 50 refugees, all of whom had, according to their descriptions, been driven over the mountains by what was going on in the Pec/Djakovica area of Kosovo. Many of them arrived in a very harrowing state - women, young children - and I was able to observe in the hospital in Bajram Curiju a number of people who had been wounded by shells, shrapnel, and gunfire, who were in various stages of illness, some one or two, I think, close to death.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The refugees to whom you spoke, all genders and ages?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yes, all genders and ages, from young babes in arms through women and some young men. The two I saw in the hospital were indeed young men and may well have received their wounds as members of the KLA. The others, however, were just ordinary families, some with truly terrible tales to tell about their passage across the mountains and about their experiences when they were driven out of their villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was there any -- and was there any pattern in what they asserted they were fleeing from?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yes, there was. They all had the same or similar stories to tell, that they were ordered out of their villages by army police. They weren't specific as to which at the time. If they stayed, they were subjected to small-arms fire. If they did not leave, they were then subjected, either the same day or sometimes later, to tank fire, artillery fire, and mortar fire. In nearly all cases, all cases I spoke to, this caused the population to leave, usually at night and nearly always together, and it caused them to embark on an extremely difficult journey through forests and overpasses of about 6.000 feet high, in the course of which they were, they said, constantly shelled on the high passes and in the forests, and as they described it - their stories were consistent but, of course, all of them hearsay - they -- many died on this journey, some of the very elderly, some of the very young, and some from the effects of shell-fire. The final decent into Albania was extremely precipitous. I saw it and inspected it close up myself. And they had some very harrowing stories to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you also concern yourself with the degree to which the KLA had become established? Did you make inquiries about that or make observations about that?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was unable to judge the extent to which KLA operations on the other side of the border were -- how extensive they were or how effective. I had, I should say, asked for permission from the Yugoslav government to enter Kosovo to see for myself, but a visa had been refused. So I was left with no option but to look at the situation from the Albanian side of the border. But I was able to see that there was an extensive passage of arms across the border. It appeared to me that the KLA were well organised. The mechanism by which they had obtained these arms was that some force, I believe but cannot prove, probably criminal organisations, bought the arms. The largest that I saw or heard of was no bigger than a 0.5 machine-gun, I think 12 -- 12-millimetre machine-gun, up to the area of Trepoje. Would it be helpful if I pointed this out on the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. We're going to distribute the map. You have the map there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, what we have made available is a large map, which I hope will have a scale helpful to the Court, folded to the correct place. A copy of that, I think, is on the overhead projector, and you will be able to follow the other.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 74.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The -- I'm sorry. Put that one on the overhead projector. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is the 1999 Kosovo planning map. Are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I am familiar with it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you would like to point out, then, on the map --

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: The area of Bajram Curiju is here. This was regarded as an extremely lawless area, where the writ of the Albanian government does not run. Indeed, I was specifically advised by Foreign Office authorities that I shouldn't go into the area because of its lawless nature. These are the mountains across which the refugees were passing, here. The village of Trepoje, which is here, was, so far as I could tell, essentially an arms supermarket. The weapons were brought up, I think probably by criminal organisations, to here. The KLA would send runners across the mountains, as it were, with orders of what they should take back, and then carried by either man-pack or by mule, and I saw both, across these high passes back into Kosovo, small arms, ammunition, grenades. No weapons that I saw or heard of larger than, as I say, a 0.5 machine-gun calibre. I drew the conclusion that the KLA were at least as visible here, organised, had support, and were -- and were exporting arms, collecting arms to foment disturbances inside Kosovo. I should perhaps add that when I returned to the -- made my report to the British Prime Minister, I recommended that if we wished to stop the actions of the KLA, which were destabilising Kosovo at the time, that the way to do this would be to assist the Albanian government to ensure that the rule of law did run in the area of Bajram Curiju and Trepoje, and that we should assist in that process. I regret that that recommendation was at the time not followed, because it is the only way that I think could have, at this stage, acted in a way which would have brought about the conditions for peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, while in Albania on this visit, and indeed at this part of your visit, were you able to keep observation, through binoculars, on the area of Junik, which we can see? Perhaps you can just point it out for us.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I was. I journeyed from Bajram Curiju through Trepoje, along the lines here - there's a very rough track up to the border crossing here - and then followed this border crossing up to a point on the Albanian Kosovo border, approximately where my marker is now, above a village which I was informed was called Gegaj, G-e-g-a-j, and this gave me a very good view of the whole area around south of Junik. There are some small villages down here. And indeed, I could see deep into Kosovo, because this is an area of plains here, almost as far as Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you observe in this four-hour period?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I was up here with some European Community Monitoring Mission - ECMM - officers who had been spending time up there, and they were able to guide me as to what I was able to see. But it was pretty self-evident what was happening. In this area here, I saw a number of VJ, Vojska Jugoslavija, tanks, a number of VJ positions, in particular, a mortar position laid out in a classic military Warsaw Pact style, and that throughout this area there were small units, probably platoons, moving about in armoured personnel carriers, APCs, and that they were bombarding, subjecting to tank fire, subjecting to mortar fire - I would estimate perhaps 82 millimetre mortars - the houses and villages around here. I would have been, I suppose, two kilometres away. I neither saw nor heard any return fire, at two kilometres, with small arms. That may not be exceptional, but you would expect to see puffs of smoke through binoculars, and I saw no return fire. I did, however, see these units engaging, it appeared to me, I'm bound to say, indiscriminately the houses and villages in this area, in a way which I could not relate to military objectives, viewed at from where I was, and I regarded as very shocking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can the witness please see our Exhibit 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Lord Ashdown, do you think you might be able to identify some of the vehicles, pieces of equipment and vehicles that you saw? If you could --

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yes. I referred to armoured personnel carriers. I can't be certain about this vehicle here, but this one, which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Number 2.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Number 1, I can't be certain about this one, but number 2, which is an armoured personnel carrier, I certainly saw at that stage. And again, unless I'm mistaken, that's a T54 tank. There were certainly those.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Number 6.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: But not, so far as I could tell from the distance I was at, those.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Number 5.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that something you did see?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Not, as I can recall, number 8. And I think probably 10, but not the others on that sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see any small artillery pieces travelling in a particular direction?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Actually, we did. I mean, the main -- the main activity going on below me, I suppose something like two kilometres away, was a tank engaging a collection of houses for an extended period of time. But looking to my north, I suddenly spotted, and I don't think it had been seen before by the ECMM monitors, a deployment of troops, which I believe to be Yugoslav army troops but I can't be absolutely certain, somewhere to the north of Neziraj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we put the map back on the -- the other map.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we put it back on the overhead projector so that people can see it.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Right. So I was here. It appeared suddenly on the ridge about, I should think, a thousand metres, a kilometre away from me. Through my binoculars, I could quite easily see troops deploying at least one gun - there may have been two - on a mountain ridge, and firing, so far as I could tell judging by the sound of the firing and the report of the shell, to the north of me; i.e., firing away from me into what I took to be - indeed there are no other possible targets there - the forests. This being consistent with the refugee stories of being subjected to shell-fire as they sought to escape Kosovo across -- through the forests and across the high mountain passes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Can we now move on from that mission, in respect to which you tell us you made a report to the Prime Minister, to the next visit, I think it was on the 26th of September, three months later, a visit that lasted some three days. On that occasion, did you meet Dr. Rugova and an Albanian delegation?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I did. I met -- I'd have to refer to my diaries if I were to go through all the meetings, but I certainly met Dr. Rugova and other representatives, Albanian representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You set out in your statement - it's more fully set out than in the summary that we have - your opinion of him as a man. Just in a sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Quiet, studious, rather withdrawn, really. He claimed to be a pacifist, and I can't comment on what contacts he may or may not have had with the KLA, but he certainly spoke in the language of a pacifist. A man who was -- I think, regarded himself and was regarded by many, particularly in rural Kosovo, as the -- the moral head of their -- of their nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you make a tour with the ambassador, UK ambassador, Brian Donnelly, and the military attache, John Crossland, of Western Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I did. I should say that that tour had been arranged and I'd indeed been collected by the British ambassador on this occasion. I had received visas from the Yugoslav government, and I was carrying with me a letter from Mr. Blair to Mr. Milosevic, then, of course, President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: We started from Pristina --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if you want to use the map --

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I think it might be --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- to make more vivid your narrative. So you can just fold it yourself.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I'll just see if I can find -- there we are. It's slightly off the map and would -- that would be a better --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're concerned, of course, with the Pristina-Pec road. And the document at which you're looking, just for the purposes of the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: This document is my diary. The diary as published. It's not -- I just want to make sure that we get the dates right. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber has no objection to --

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: On the 27th and the 28th. On the 27th, we left Pristina here and travelled on the main road to Pec. There's Pec up here. And the main road runs here, and we were, of course, travelling in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. What observations did you make in late September of 1998 about the condition of the villages you passed; about farm animals, crops, and the like?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Well, all the way along this road, there was clear evidence of very substantial burning of properties. The properties were, I think, almost all without exception, destroyed, uninhabited, shops on the sides of the road and in the small hamlets burnt, all the properties roofless, having been set on fire, evidence of gunfire, shell holes, small-arms holes. I stopped -- can't be absolutely certain, I regret for the Court, but I stopped on this road, I think somewhere around about the Klina crossing. This is Klina here. Somewhere around about here. I mean, purely at random, simply so as to be able to take a look at one of these hamlets for myself. It consisted of I suppose half a dozen houses, perhaps to a dozen houses, a small group of shops which I had suspected being an auto repair shop and a television shop, and some purely agricultural houses. The cattle were either dead and bloated from putrefaction, having been shot, or roaming the fields. The houses seemed to me to have been systematically burnt. In one house I went into, there was a store of grain which was, it appeared to me and I was told by those who accompanied me, was clearly a store of grain for next year's planting - i.e., not grain to be eaten but grain to be planted - that had been set on fire, destroyed by water, and trashed. And I can only describe this village like every other I saw, as being utterly trashed, nobody living there, and all means of livelihood in the village had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were there any local residents to whom you were able to speak?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: No. They'd all gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The place was deserted?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Deserted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you -- did you reach Pec?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: We did. We stopped for coffee in Pec, as I recall, and Pec struck me as being nervous but quiet. I mean, there was no immediate evidence of destruction in the Pec area. Indeed, if I recall correctly, close where we had coffee there were a couple of Albanians who were busy sawing up wood for winter, and there was every sign of a normal Balkan town preparing for the season ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think you visited a monastery.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yes. I particularly wanted to be able to see, as it were, both sides of the story, and so we visited the Decani monastery, which is approximately here. It's a wonderful jewel of a Serbian monastery. I was informed, and this was confirmed by everybody else, that to the nation of Serbia, to Serbs, this area is rather like Canterbury is to Britain, their centre of religious importance. It's a very beautiful monastery, and I was rather privileged of being shown around by one of the monks, Father Sava, and, if I recall, afterwards enjoying a glass of slivovitz with him. But it was in perfect condition and that stage remains today, I'm informed, but I can't be certain of that, being completely untouched. I fear the same cannot be said of the villages down the Pec-Djakovica road. It might be helpful if I were just to say that in one of these, a place called Prilep, the village was completely destroyed. In my opinion and that of the military attache with me, it had been subject not only to tank and artillery fire but almost certainly to rocket fire, aircraft rockets, in our opinion, and there was certainly sufficient bits of ordnance, bits of rocket lying around to indicate that. In this village, I came across an elderly woman and her young daughter living in the remains of a house. She explained to me that she came there every day from staying with her neighbours 14 or so kilometres away, having been driven out of her village, to look after the farm animals, and she explained to me how she was preparing to live in these very miserable conditions, the whole of the village around her having been destroyed during the winter. I asked whether any men came back, and she said yes, some had dared to. She described a situation where two men had come back and done something nobody else had dared to do, which was to spend the night in the village. And they had returned the next day to find both dead, with their throats cut.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we -- just one minute. Before you got to Prilep, had you observed Albanian-dominated villages in the area of Decani?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yes. Decani too was in a very bad state, though I think Prilep was the worst of them. In fairness, I think it's important to say that I did hear a story that, close to Prilep, some Serb policemen had been killed in a recent ambush, presumably by the KLA, and the condition of Prilep was the result of reprisals as a result of that military action.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you visit a Serb community near Decani and get an account of KLA activity?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I did, actually. When I was on my previous visit, I noticed a group of sparkling new houses in a -- what I can only describe as a rather -- housing estate you would have recognised on the outskirts of any British town, in the area not of Decani but of Junik. If you remember, I was watching the Junik area. And I was informed on my previous visit that this was the home of Serb refugees from the Krajina in Croatia. And so I wanted to see what condition they were in, and indeed I was able to see the same houses I had seen in my earlier visit. They were indeed occupied by Serbs, and although I was told stories that they too had been subjected to KLA attack, I inspected the outside of the houses carefully and only saw occasional -- I mean occasional -- by "occasional," I mean four or five single bullet holes in the outside. They were at the time being visited by Serb police members of the -- I suspect of the Ministry of Interior police, or MUP, but they could have been Serb irregular units because they were often dressed in very similar uniforms. I have to say that -- that I saw no evidence there of a community significantly under threat. That is not to say that some Serbs had not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. been taken by the KLA, murdered by the KLA. I condemned that at the time. It is not to say that there were Serb policemen who were not subject to attack, it is not to say that there were not ambushes, but this community of houses did not appear to me to be having experienced severe threats or having experienced significant or any, indeed, attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you visited some sites of alleged deaths of both Serbs and burial sites of Albanians?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yes. I was again concerned to make sure that I got a balanced picture and asked to be taken -- was taken to the site of an alleged Serb execution. I say "alleged" because I can't prove otherwise, but I have presented my evidence of this to the International Tribunal. I'm convinced that an execution did take place there. It was in a culvert of a stream. I was informed that six or seven Serbs had been executed there. Their bodies had been in the stream but were not there when I got there, but they had been observed by Major Crossland. Judging by the empty bullet cases that I found there, 7.62 short magazine, Chinese origin shell cases, distributed in such a fashion that there appeared to be four or five firing points, leading me to believe that, (a), these were conducted by people with Chinese-manufacture Kalashnikov weapons, a weapon that was very commonly used by the KLA, and judging by the firing points, this had not been the result of a battle but was indeed an execution. I believe a -- I believe a couple or three days later, Mr. Milutinovic from the Serbian government also visited this site.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you were able to go to the hills above Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Well, we next went to Orahovac. I just need to find it. This map isn't necessarily as absolutely clear. Orahovac is here, an area famous for its wine growing, where we were informed that some Albanians had been killed recently. We were taken to a local refuse dump close to a cemetery, contiguous with the cemetery, really, and there were coffins sticking out of the refuse and a strong smell of putrefaction, leading me to believe that however they got there, there were bodies hastily buried here, and everything was consistent with the story that I had been heard -- I had heard. We then passed along this road here, heading for Suva Reka, through the village of Studencane, which is here. I should explain that this is a road with high mountains on the left-hand side and the valleys of Kosovo stretching south down here. As we came round the corner, I would imagine this corner of the road, I was able to see beyond Suva Reka the whole of this valley here, which forms a sort of amphitheatre for this area here. And I am bound to say I was deeply shocked by what I saw, as indeed was the British ambassador, the British ambassador having been informed that the Yugoslav government had said that the operations which were continuing against the Drenica villages of Kosovo had stopped the previous day. What we -- or two days previously. What we were presented with was an entire amphitheatre of hills in which every village was ablaze, and we saw and heard the reports of shell-fire, saw the explosions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you able to gauge the weapons that were being used?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I've -- I have some experience in these matters. Perhaps not as much as Colonel Crossland, but we concluded that the weapons being used here were artillery. In our judgement, artillery being fired from the Dolje Blace feature. This is a feature that runs down in this direction. Dolje is there, some seven to ten kilometres from the villages concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: And we could hear the -- not only see the strike of the shells, but we could hear the boom of the artillery. And our conclusion was that the weapons being used here probably were the full range of weapons available to an armoured brigade. T54 tanks, probably. Certainly there was tank fire. Artillery, certainly 120 millimetre, and we believed perhaps as big as 150 millimetre. And judging by the strikes we were able to see in these villages, mortars. And again, the strike of a mortar is very particular as against an artillery shell, and we estimated mortars of 82 millimetre mortars and perhaps 120 millimetre mortars as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, to conclude this passage of evidence, there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it's now after 5.00 and we need to adjourn. We'll look at that in the morning. This witness has to finish by a certain time tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Lunchtime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Lunchtime. Well, you will leave adequate time for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course. The balance will not take very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Lord Ashdown, we're going to adjourn now. Would you remember in this adjournment and any other there may be not to speak to anybody about your evidence, including the Prosecution team, until it's over. Could you be back, please, at half past nine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 5.02 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 15th day of March, 2002, at 9.30 a.m.
